claim: Litomosoides sigmodontis is a rodent filarial nematode used to model the host response to infection with filarial parasites of humans such as Onchocerca volvulus and Wuchereria bancrofti.
source: Litomosoides sigmodontis is a rodent filarial nematode which is used to model the host response to infection with filarial parasites of humans such as Onchocerca volvulus and Wuchereria bancrofti (Hoffmann et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2000

claim: Infective L3 stage larvae take 3–6 days to migrate from the skin to the pleural cavity.
source: Infective L3 stage larvae take 3–6 days to migrate from the skin to the pleural cavity, where they remain for the duration of infection.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about L. sigmodontis infection

claim: In susceptible BALB/c mice, L. sigmodontis parasites mature, mate and produce microfilariae that circulate in the bloodstream from ~day 55 post infection.
source: In susceptible BALB/c mice parasites mature, mate and produce microfilariae that circulate in the bloodstream from ~day 55 post infection (pi).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about BALB/c susceptibility

claim: C57BL/6 mice are considered resistant to L. sigmodontis because the number of adult nematodes recoverable from the pleural cavity declines from ~day 22–55 and parasites do not reach sexual maturity or produce microfilariae.
source: In contrast to BALB/c mice, C57BL/6 mice are considered resistant because the number of adult nematodes recoverable from the pleural cavity declines from ~day 22–55 and parasites do not reach sexual maturity or produce microfilariae (Hoffmann et al., 2000; Graham et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2000 and Graham et al., 2005

claim: The absence of IL-4 renders C57BL/6 mice susceptible to L. sigmodontis infection, with blood microfilariae detectable at day 60 pi.
source: The absence of IL-4, the central cytokine of type two immunity, renders C57BL/6 mice susceptible to L. sigmodontis infection, with blood microfilariae detectable at day 60 pi (Le Goff et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Le Goff et al., 2002

claim: In response to IL-4Rα stimulation, macrophages assume an M(IL-4) activation phenotype characterised by the expression of molecules RELMα, YM1 and arginase-1.
source: In response to IL-4Rα stimulation MΦ assume an M(IL-4) activation phenotype characterised by the expression of molecules RELMα, YM1 and arginase-1 (Stein et al., 1992; Doyle et al., 1994; Loke et al., 2002; Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Stein et al., 1992; Doyle et al., 1994; Loke et al., 2002; Murray et al., 2014

claim: M(IL-4) macrophages have been implicated in nematode killing.
source: M(IL-4) have been implicated in nematode killing (Anthony et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2008; Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Bonne-Année et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Anthony et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2008; Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Bonne-Année et al., 2013

claim: M(IL-4) macrophages have been implicated in suppression of the TH2 immune response.
source: M(IL-4) have been implicated in nematode killing (Anthony et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2008; Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Bonne-Année et al., 2013) but paradoxically also in suppression of the TH2 immune response (Nair et al., 2009; Pesce et al., 2009b; Pesce et al., 2009a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nair et al., 2009; Pesce et al., 2009b; Pesce et al., 2009a

claim: IL-4 induces the proliferative expansion of F4/80hi resident macrophages in the pleural cavity during L. sigmodontis infection, with minimal blood monocyte recruitment.
source: We have previously reported that IL-4 induces the proliferative expansion of F4/80hi resident MΦ (resMΦ) in the pleural cavity during L. sigmodontis infection, with minimal blood monocyte recruitment (Jenkins et al., 2011; Jenkins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jenkins et al., 2011; Jenkins et al., 2013

claim: F4/80hi resident macrophages of the serous cavities are initially derived from F4/80hi yolk-sac and foetal liver macrophages, prior to the establishment of haematopoietic stem cells.
source: F4/80hi resMΦ of the serous cavities are initially derived from F4/80hi yolk-sac and foetal liver MΦ, prior to the establishment of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) which give rise to F4/80lo bone marrow derived MΦ (bmMΦ) (Yona et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2012; Ginhoux et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yona et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2012; Ginhoux et al., 2010

claim: Haematopoietic stem cells give rise to F4/80lo bone marrow derived macrophages.
source: F4/80hi resMΦ of the serous cavities are initially derived from F4/80hi yolk-sac and foetal liver MΦ, prior to the establishment of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) which give rise to F4/80lo bone marrow derived MΦ (bmMΦ) (Yona et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2012; Ginhoux et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yona et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2012; Ginhoux et al., 2010

claim: F4/80hi resident macrophages and recently recruited F4/80lo bone marrow-derived macrophages possess distinct M(IL-4) activation profiles upon stimulation with IL-4.
source: F4/80hi resMΦ and recently recruited F4/80lo bmMΦ possess distinct M(IL-4) activation profiles upon stimulation with IL-4 (Gundra et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gundra et al., 2014

claim: As early as day 11 post infection, there were significantly more cells isolated from the pleural cavity of resistant C57BL/6 mice compared to susceptible BALB/c mice.
source: As early as day 11 pi there were significantly more cells isolated from the pleural cavity of resistant C57BL/6 mice as compared to susceptible BALB/c mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The greater cellularity in C57BL/6 mice at day 11 post infection was due predominantly to significantly higher macrophage numbers along with more B cells.
source: This greater cellularity was due predominantly to significantly higher MΦ numbers along with more B cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Neutrophil numbers were significantly higher in infected C57BL/6 mice at day 28 and 35 post infection but represented less than 1% of the total cells.
source: Neutrophil numbers were significantly higher in infected C57BL/6 mice at day 28 and 35 pi but represented less than 1% of the total cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: Only eosinophils and T cells were significantly higher in BALB/c mice and only at day 50 post infection.
source: Only eosinophils and T cells were significantly higher in BALB/c mice and only at day 50, a difference likely due to the presence of parasites in BALB/c but not C57BL/6 mice at the later time point.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: The enhanced macrophage number observed in C57BL/6 mice compared to BALB/c mice was reflective of an expanded F4/80hi population.
source: This gating strategy revealed that the enhanced MΦ number observed in C57BL/6 mice as compared to BALB/c mice was reflective of an expanded F4/80hi population (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: There were more F4/80lo macrophages in the C57BL/6 strain but only at day 11 post infection.
source: There were also more F4/80lo MΦ in the C57BL/6 strain but only at day 11 pi.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: F4/80lo macrophage numbers did not differ significantly between C57BL/6 and BALB/c strains throughout the remainder of the infection time course after day 11.
source: F4/80lo MΦ numbers did not differ significantly between strains throughout the remainder of the time course (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: C57BL/6 mice displayed increased numbers of monocytes throughout the infection compared to their naïve controls.
source: Notably, although C57BL/6 mice displayed increased numbers of monocytes throughout the infection as compared to their naïve controls, BALB/c mice were marked by a significant influx of Ly6C+ monocytes first observed at day 35 pi (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: BALB/c mice were marked by a significant influx of Ly6C+ monocytes first observed at day 35 post infection.
source: Notably, although C57BL/6 mice displayed increased numbers of monocytes throughout the infection as compared to their naïve controls, BALB/c mice were marked by a significant influx of Ly6C+ monocytes first observed at day 35 pi (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In naïve C57BL/6 control mice, the F4/80hi population constituted 80–90% of the total macrophage population from 8 to 15 weeks of age.
source: In naïve C57BL/6 control mice the F4/80hi population constituted 80–90% of the total MΦ population from 8 to 15 weeks of age (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The remaining 10–20% of the macrophage compartment in naïve C57BL/6 mice was composed of F4/80lo macrophages, with almost negligible contribution of monocytes.
source: The remaining 10–20% of the MΦ compartment was composed of F4/80lo MΦ, with almost negligible contribution of monocytes in the C57BL/6 strain (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The proportion of F4/80hi cells contributing to the macrophage pool in naïve C57BL/6 mice declined slightly with age from 87 ± 3% to 73 ± 3%.
source: Interestingly, the proportion of F4/80hi cells contributing to the MΦ pool in naïve C57BL/6 mice declined slightly with age (87 ± 3% to 73 ± 3%) and infection prevented this age-related decline, maintaining the F4/80hi population at ~90% of the total MΦ pool (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Infection prevented the age-related decline of F4/80hi cells in C57BL/6 mice, maintaining the F4/80hi population at ~90% of the total macrophage pool.
source: Interestingly, the proportion of F4/80hi cells contributing to the MΦ pool in naïve C57BL/6 mice declined slightly with age (87 ± 3% to 73 ± 3%) and infection prevented this age-related decline, maintaining the F4/80hi population at ~90% of the total MΦ pool (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The transcription factor GATA6 and cell surface protein CD102 are markers of residency expressed by the F4/80hi macrophage population within the peritoneal and pleural spaces of C57BL/6 mice.
source: The transcription factor GATA6 and cell surface protein CD102 have been identified as markers of residency expressed by the F4/80hi MΦ population within the peritoneal and pleural spaces of C57BL/6 mice (Okabe and Medzhitov, 2014; Rosas et al., 2014; Bain et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okabe and Medzhitov, 2014; Rosas et al., 2014; Bain et al., 2016

claim: The F4/80hi population in C57BL/6 mice was positive for GATA6 and CD102.
source: Consistent with these reports the F4/80hi population in C57BL/6 mice was positive for GATA6 and CD102 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In naïve C57BL/6 mice, ~80–90% of the total macrophage pool was positive for GATA6 and CD102 at 8 weeks of age or day 11 post infection.
source: Consistent with these reports the F4/80hi population in C57BL/6 mice was positive for GATA6 and CD102 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) which was reflected in ~80–90% of the total MΦ pool being positive for GATA6 and CD102 at 8 weeks of age or d11 pi (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In naïve C57BL/6 mice, the percentage of macrophages expressing GATA6 was significantly reduced by 15 weeks of age.
source: In naïve C57BL/6 mice, the percentage of MΦ expressing GATA6 was significantly reduced by 15 weeks of age (Figure 2C) reflective of the age-related decline in the proportion of F4/80hi cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2B

claim: There was no decline in GATA6 expression within the macrophage compartment of infected C57BL/6 mice.
source: In contrast, there was no decline in GATA6 within the MΦ compartment of infected C57BL/6 mice and CD102 expression was sustained at a higher level in infected mice (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: CD102 expression was sustained at a higher level in infected C57BL/6 mice.
source: In contrast, there was no decline in GATA6 within the MΦ compartment of infected C57BL/6 mice and CD102 expression was sustained at a higher level in infected mice (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In BALB/c mice, the F4/80hi population represented 70–80% of the macrophage compartment at 8 weeks of age/day 11 post infection, slightly lower than in the C57BL/6 strain.
source: The MΦ dynamics of the BALB/c strain were distinct from the outset, with the F4/80hi population representing 70–80% of the MΦ compartment at 8 weeks of age/day 11 pi, slightly lower than what was observed in the C57BL/6 strain (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: A more pronounced decline in the proportion of F4/80hi cells contributing to the total macrophage compartment was observed in both naïve and infected BALB/c mice over the time course.
source: A more pronounced decline in the proportion of F4/80hi cells contributing to the total MΦ compartment was observed in both naïve and infected BALB/c mice over the time course.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: The decline in F4/80hi cells in BALB/c mice was marked by a corresponding increase in the percentage of F4/80lo macrophages in the cavity.
source: This decline was marked by a corresponding increase in the percentage of F4/80lo MΦ in the cavity (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: L. sigmodontis infection in the BALB/c strain did not prevent the age-related decrease in the proportion of F4/80hi cells.
source: In contrast to C57BL/6 mice, L. sigmodontis infection in the BALB/c strain did not prevent the age-related decrease in the proportion of F4/80hi cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: By day 50 post infection in the BALB/c strain, F4/80lo macrophages and monocytes represent >50% of the myeloid pool.
source: As a result, by day 50 pi in the BALB/c strain, F4/80lo MΦ and monocytes represent >50% of the myeloid pool (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The proportion of myeloid cells expressing residency markers GATA6 and CD102 declined significantly over the time course in both naïve and infected BALB/c mice.
source: Consequently, the proportion of myeloid cells expressing residency markers GATA6 and CD102 declined significantly over the time course in both naïve and infected BALB/c mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: F4/80hi macrophage proliferation peaked above naive levels at day 11 post infection only.
source: Of the time points measured, F4/80hi resMΦ proliferation peaked above naive levels at day 11 pi only (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: F4/80hi macrophage proliferation at day 11 post infection was significantly greater in the C57BL/6 strain compared to BALB/c.
source: Of the time points measured, F4/80hi resMΦ proliferation peaked above naive levels at day 11 pi only (Figure 3A) and was significantly greater in the C57BL/6 strain compared to BALB/c (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: F4/80hi macrophage expansion at day 28 post infection was not significantly altered in Ccr2-/- C57BL/6 mice.
source: Experiments in Ccr2-/- C57BL/6 mice demonstrated that F4/80hi MΦ expansion at d28 pi was not significantly altered making it unlikely that bone marrow derived cells were contributing to the increased numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: Approximately 50% of the F4/80hi population was derived from the bone marrow by 23 weeks of age in naïve and infected C57BL/6 animals at day 35 post infection.
source: We were initially surprised to find that ~50% of the F4/80hi population was derived from the bone marrow by 23 weeks of age in naïve and infected animals at day 35 pi.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bone marrow chimera experiments

claim: Bone marrow chimerism in the F4/80hi population increased to ~80% over two weeks from day 35 to day 50 post infection.
source: Over the next two weeks chimerism increased further to ~80% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Despite near identical chimerism between infected and naïve C57BL/6 mice at both day 35 and day 50, infected mice possessed a macrophage population size that was 27-fold larger.
source: Critically, despite near identical chimerism between infected and naïve mice at both day 35 and day 50, infected mice possessed a MΦ population size that was 27-fold larger (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The increased contribution of bone marrow-derived macrophages to the F4/80hi pool was an age-related phenomenon, the rate of which was not accelerated by nematode infection.
source: Thus the increased contribution of bmMΦ to the F4/80hi pool was an age related phenomena, the rate of which was not accelerated by nematode infection.
evidence: Inferred from bone marrow chimera data showing similar chimerism in infected and naïve mice

claim: Bain et al., 2016 showed a gradual replenishment of the pleural F4/80hi population by bone marrow-derived macrophages with age.
source: This data is supported by the findings of Bain et al., 2016 showing a gradual replenishment of the pleural F4/80hi population by bmMΦ with age (Bain et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bain et al., 2016

claim: In the study by Bain et al., 2016, the level of bone marrow cell contribution to the pleural macrophage compartment is ~50% by 19 weeks of age.
source: In that study, the level of bone marrow cell contribution to the pleural MΦ compartment is ~50% by 19 weeks of age.
evidence: Referencing findings from Bain et al., 2016

claim: All F4/80hi macrophages were positive for residency markers GATA6 and CD102.
source: All of F4/80hi MΦ were positive for residency markers GATA6 and CD102 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Donor-derived F4/80hi macrophages were equally capable of expressing residency markers GATA6 and CD102 as host-derived cells in both naïve and infected C57BL/6 mice.
source: Comparison of GATA6 and CD102 expression by donor- and host-derived F4/80hi MΦ within naïve and infected C57BL/6 mice revealed that donor-derived cells were equally capable of expressing these residency markers as host-derived cells (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E

claim: Only 46 ± 1.6% of the F4/80hi population was TIM4+ in naïve C57BL/6 animals aged 23–25 weeks.
source: Unlike GATA6 and CD102, which uniformly marked the F4/80hi population, only 46 ± 1.6% of the F4/80hi population was TIM4+ in naïve animals aged 23–25 weeks (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: In naïve C57BL/6 controls at 25 weeks of age, an equal proportion of donor and host F4/80hi cells were negative for Tim-4.
source: In naïve controls at 25 weeks of age, an equal proportion of donor and host F4/80hi cells were negative for Tim-4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: Even long-lived bone marrow derived cells do not universally take on Tim4 expression in the steady state.
source: This data is consistent with the finding of Bain et al., 2016 that even long-lived bone marrow derived cells do not universally take on Tim4 expression in the steady state (Bain et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bain et al., 2016

claim: L. sigmodontis infection induced TIM4 expression on the F4/80hi population, with 76 ± 4% staining TIM4 positive at day 35 and 50 post infection.
source: The striking result here was that L. sigmodontis infection induced TIM4 expression on the F4/80hi population, with 76 ± 4% staining TIM4 positive at day 35 and 50 pi (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: By day 50 post infection, the majority of both donor and host F4/80hi cells expressed Tim4.
source: The striking result here was that L. sigmodontis infection induced TIM4 expression on the F4/80hi population, with 76 ± 4% staining TIM4 positive at day 35 and 50 pi (Figure 3F), and by day 50 Tim4 expression more closely resembled that of GATA6 and CD102 with the majority of both donor and host F4/80hi cells expressing Tim4 (Figure 3F&G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: Bain et al., 2016 highlighted that in naïve mice RELMα is expressed by bone marrow precursors to the F4/80hi resident macrophage pool and that RELMα transiently marks cells of monocytic origin.
source: Bain et al., 2016 have recently highlighted that in naïve mice RELMα is expressed by bone marrow precursors (F4/80loMHCII+CSF1R+) to the F4/80hi resMΦ pool and that RELMα transiently marks cells of monocytic origin.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bain et al., 2016

claim: Approximately 60% of the F4/80lo macrophages were RELMα positive in naïve C57BL/6 mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed ~60 and~80% of the F4/80lo MΦ were RELMα positive in naïve C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice respectively, while ~10% and ~50% were RELMα positive in the respective F4/80hi populations (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Approximately 80% of the F4/80lo macrophages were RELMα positive in naïve BALB/c mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed ~60 and~80% of the F4/80lo MΦ were RELMα positive in naïve C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice respectively, while ~10% and ~50% were RELMα positive in the respective F4/80hi populations (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Approximately 10% of the F4/80hi population was RELMα positive in naïve C57BL/6 mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed ~60 and~80% of the F4/80lo MΦ were RELMα positive in naïve C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice respectively, while ~10% and ~50% were RELMα positive in the respective F4/80hi populations (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Approximately 50% of the F4/80hi population was RELMα positive in naïve BALB/c mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed ~60 and~80% of the F4/80lo MΦ were RELMα positive in naïve C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice respectively, while ~10% and ~50% were RELMα positive in the respective F4/80hi populations (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Upon infection of both C57BL/6 and BALB/c strains, almost all macrophages regardless of phenotype expressed RELMα.
source: However, upon infection of both strains almost all MΦ regardless of phenotype expressed RELMα (Figure 4A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The ability of IL-4Rα signaling to induce RELMα expression is independent of strain or origin.
source: However, upon infection of both strains almost all MΦ regardless of phenotype expressed RELMα (Figure 4A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), a reflection of the ability of IL-4Rα signaling to induce RELMα expression independent of strain or origin (Jenkins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jenkins et al., 2013 and experimental data

claim: The immunosuppressive molecule programmed cell death ligand 2 (PD-L2) is induced by IL-4 and is preferentially expressed by F4/80lo M(IL-4).
source: Like RELMα, the immunosuppressive molecule programmed cell death ligand 2 (PD-L2) is induced by IL-4 but in contrast to RELMα, is preferentially expressed by F4/80lo M(IL-4) (Gundra et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gundra et al., 2014

claim: PD-L2 is permanently downregulated by F4/80lo M(IL-4) upon integration into the resident pool even in the face of subsequent IL-4Rα signaling.
source: In addition, PD-L2 is permanently downregulated by F4/80lo M(IL-4) upon integration into the resident pool even in the face of subsequent IL-4Rα signaling (Gundra et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gundra et al., 2017

claim: PD-L2 expression was upregulated by all macrophage sub-populations of infected BALB/c mice compared to naïve controls.
source: PD-L2 expression was upregulated by all MΦ sub-populations of infected BALB/c mice compared to naïve controls (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Infected C57BL/6 mice exhibited significantly lower frequencies of PD-L2+ macrophages relative to BALB/c mice.
source: PD-L2 expression was upregulated by all MΦ sub-populations of infected BALB/c mice compared to naïve controls (Figure 4B) whereas infected C57BL/6 mice exhibited significantly lower frequencies of PD-L2+ MΦs relative to BALB/c mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: There was negligible detection of PD-L2 expression by the F4/80hi population of C57BL/6 mice at day 50 post infection.
source: Indeed, there was negligible detection of PD-L2 expression by the F4/80hi population of C57BL/6 mice at day 50 pi (Figure 4B), despite being ~80% bone marrow derived (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3B

claim: Successful integration into the resident niche results in an inability to upregulate PD-L2 in response to helminth infection.
source: This provides additional evidence that successful integration into the resident niche results in an inability to upregulate PD-L2 in response to helminth infection, consistent with recent findings (Gundra et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Gundra et al., 2017

claim: PD-1 is highly expressed on TH2 cells during chronic L. sigmodontis infection of susceptible BALB/c mice.
source: PD-L2 has specific relevance to L. sigmodontis, where its ligand PD-1 is highly expressed on TH2 cells during chronic infection of susceptible BALB/c mice.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about PD-1 expression

claim: PD-1/PD-L2 interaction induces a state of TH2 cell-intrinsic hypo-responsiveness characterized by significantly diminished production of TH2 signature cytokines IL-4 and IL-5.
source: In this setting, PD-1/PD-L2 interaction induces a state of TH2 cell-intrinsic hypo-responsiveness that is characterised by significantly diminished production of TH2 signature cytokines IL-4 and IL-5 (van der Werf et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Werf et al., 2013

claim: Expression of the TH2 master transcription factor GATA3 was significantly greater in CD4+ T cells isolated from the pleural cavity of C57BL/6 mice compared with BALB/c at day 50 post infection.
source: Expression of the TH2 master transcription factor GATA3 was significantly greater in CD4+ T cells isolated from the pleural cavity of C57BL/6 mice compared with BALB/c (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: No significant difference in expression of IL-4 or IL-5 by GATA3+CD4+ cells was detected between C57BL/6 and BALB/c mice at day 50 post infection.
source: Expression of the TH2 master transcription factor GATA3 was significantly greater in CD4+ T cells isolated from the pleural cavity of C57BL/6 mice compared with BALB/c (Figure 4C) although no significant difference in expression of IL-4 or IL-5 by GATA3+CD4+ cells was detected (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: There was a significantly greater proportion of IFN-γ producing CD4+ cells from infected BALB/c mice compared to C57BL/6 mice at day 50 post infection.
source: Interestingly however, there was a significantly greater proportion of IFN-γ producing CD4+ cells from infected BALB/c mice compared to C57BL/6 mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between the percentage of PD-L2+ macrophages and worm recovery rate.
source: Notably, there was a strong positive correlation between the percentage of PD-L2+ MΦ and worm recovery rate (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Anti-CCR2 antibody treatment from day 31–34 post infection successfully prevented the influx of monocytes into the pleural cavity of BALB/c mice.
source: Antibody treatment in this time frame successfully prevented the influx of monocytes into the pleural cavity, resulting in the F4/80hi population representing ~80% of the total MΦ compartment (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Inhibiting monocyte infiltration resulted in significantly increased worm killing in the normally susceptible BALB/c mice.
source: Inhibiting monocyte infiltration resulted in significantly increased worm killing in the normally susceptible BALB/c mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: In the anti-CCR2 treated group, 29% of the mice had no parasites compared to 5% in the rat IgG treated group.
source: In the anti-CCR2 treated group 29% of the mice had no parasites compared to 5% in the rat IgG treated group, a striking effect given the BALB/c mice typically have not cleared the infection until ~day 90 pi.
evidence: Supported by experimental data referenced in the text

claim: Anti-CCR2 treatment did not affect the number of F4/80hi macrophages in the cavity.
source: Anti-CCR2 treatment did not affect the number of F4/80hi MΦ in the cavity, but significantly reduced F4/80lo MΦ and depleted monocytes (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Anti-CCR2 treatment significantly reduced F4/80lo macrophages and depleted monocytes.
source: Anti-CCR2 treatment did not affect the number of F4/80hi MΦ in the cavity, but significantly reduced F4/80lo MΦ and depleted monocytes (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: There was no significant difference in the percentage or number of PD-L2+ macrophages between anti-CCR2 treated and Rat IgG treated controls at day 35 post infection.
source: The difference in parasite killing could not readily be attributed to PD-L2, however, as there was no significant difference in the percentage or number of PD-L2+ MΦ between anti-CCR2 treated and Rat IgG treated controls at this time point (Figure 5E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: No difference was detected in the number of pleural cavity CD4+GATA3+ TH2 cells between control and monocyte depleted BALB/c mice.
source: While no difference was detected in the number of pleural cavity CD4+GATA3+ TH2 cells between control and monocyte depleted mice (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The proportion of CD4+GATA3+TH2 cells producing IL-4 in monocyte depleted BALB/c mice was significantly enhanced.
source: While no difference was detected in the number of pleural cavity CD4+GATA3+ TH2 cells between control and monocyte depleted mice (Figure 5F), the proportion of CD4+GATA3+TH2 cells producing IL-4 in monocyte depleted mice was significantly enhanced (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The frequency of IL-5+ and IFN-γ+ cells were not significantly altered by monocyte depletion in BALB/c mice.
source: The frequency of IL-5+ and IFN-γ+ cells were not significantly altered (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Resistance against L. sigmodontis in C57BL/6 mice was associated with the predominance of an M(IL-4) F4/80hiGATA6+CD102+ resident macrophage population that accumulated through proliferation of the existing population.
source: Resistance against L. sigmodontis in C57BL/6 mice was associated with the predominance of an M(IL-4) F4/80hiGATA6+CD102+ resMΦ population that accumulated through proliferation of the existing population.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages successfully integrated into the resident macrophage niche, as defined by GATA6 and CD102 expression in both naïve and infected C57BL/6 animals.
source: Here we show that bmMΦ successfully integrated into the resMΦ niche, as defined by GATA6 and CD102 expression in both naïve and infected animals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: Resident macrophages of the serous cavity are replenished from the bone marrow in an age-dependent manner.
source: This data re-enforces the finding that resMΦ of the serous cavity are replenished from the bone marrow in an age-dependent manner (Bain et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bain et al., 2016 and experimental data from this study

claim: Helminth infection does not alter the homeostatic rate of age-dependent replenishment of resident macrophages.
source: We further show that despite a dramatic increase in MΦ number within the cavity as well as infection-dependent changes in phenotype, helminth infection does not alter the homeostatic rate of age-dependent replenishment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: Resistance in C57BL/6 mice was associated with a greater degree of pleural B cell accumulation.
source: Resistance was also associated with a greater degree of pleural B cell accumulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: B cells and their antibody products play a central role in anti-nematode immunity.
source: B cells and their antibody products play a central role in anti-nematode immunity (Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Rajan et al., 2005; Carter et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Rajan et al., 2005; Carter et al., 2007

claim: During primary L. sigmodontis infection, pleural cavity B cells proliferate and produce antigen-specific IgM.
source: B cells and their antibody products play a central role in anti-nematode immunity (Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013; Rajan et al., 2005; Carter et al., 2007) and we recently reported that during primary L. sigmodontis infection, pleural cavity B cells proliferate and produce antigen-specific IgM (Jackson-Jones et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jackson-Jones et al., 2016

claim: Collaboration between macrophages and antibodies to trap and kill invading larvae has been demonstrated during secondary H. polygurus infection.
source: Collaboration between MΦ and antibodies to trap and kill invading larvae has been demonstrated during secondary H. polygurus infection (Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Esser-von Bieren et al., 2013

claim: Susceptibility in the BALB/c strain was marked by significantly less F4/80hi macrophage proliferation.
source: Susceptibility in the BALB/c strain was marked by significantly less F4/80hi macrophage proliferation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: The F4/80hiGATA6+CD102+ resident macrophage population within both naïve and infected BALB/c mice diminished with age while the percentage of bone marrow-derived macrophages contributing to the macrophage compartment increased.
source: Additionally, the F4/80hiGATA6+CD102+ resMΦ population within both naïve and infected BALB/c mice diminished with age while the percentage of bmMΦ contributing to the MΦ compartment increased.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: The dynamics of bone marrow-derived macrophages in BALB/c mice are suggestive of an inability of influxing bone marrow-derived macrophages to integrate into the resident macrophage niche.
source: Such dynamics are suggestive of an inability of influxing bmMΦ to integrate into the resMΦ niche of BALB/c mice and could reflect a deficit in local retinoic acid.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing poor integration markers in BALB/c mice

claim: A recent study highlighted the inability of bone marrow-derived macrophages to integrate into the resident macrophage niche of C57BL/6 mice on a Vitamin A deficient diet.
source: Indeed a recent study has highlighted the inability bmMΦ to integrate into the resMΦ niche of C57BL/6 mice on a Vitamin A deficient diet (Gundra et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gundra et al., 2017

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages in BALB/c mice may be transcriptionally silenced at the GATA6 locus as has been noted for thioglycollate elicited macrophages.
source: Alternatively bmMΦ in BALB/c mice may be transcriptionally silenced at the GATA6 locus as has been noted for thioglycollate elicited MΦ (Okabe and Medzhitov, 2014).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation to Okabe and Medzhitov, 2014

claim: Infection in the BALB/c strain was marked by an influx of Ly6C+ monocytes by day 35 post infection, resulting in a large proportion of the myeloid compartment possessing a recently recruited F4/80loMHCIIhi phenotype by day 50 post infection.
source: Infection in the BALB/c strain was also marked by an influx of Ly6C+ monocytes by day 35 pi. resulting in a large proportion of the myeloid compartment possessing a recently recruited F4/80loMHCIIhi phenotype by day 50 pi.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: Recently recruited F4/80loMHCIIhi cells preferentially express PD-L2.
source: Because these cells preferentially express PD-L2 (Gundra et al., 2014), there was also a greater degree of PD-L2 expression upon M(IL-4) activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gundra et al., 2014

claim: Monocyte depletion prior to day 35 post infection revealed an immunosuppressive role for monocytes and F4/80lo M(IL-4) during L. sigmodontis infection, with an enhanced TH2 profile.
source: Monocyte depletion prior to day 35 pi revealed an immunosuppressive role for monocytes and F4/80lo M(IL-4) during L. sigmodontis infection, with an enhanced TH2 profile.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: A similar influx of monocytes that mature into PD-L2+ bone marrow-derived macrophages is seen in the liver of S. mansoni infected mice.
source: It is notable that a similar influx of monocytes that mature into PD-L2+ bmMΦ is seen in the liver of S. mansoni infected mice (Pearce and MacDonald, 2002; Nascimento et al., 2014; Gundra et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearce and MacDonald, 2002; Nascimento et al., 2014; Gundra et al., 2014

claim: Depletion of immunosuppressive bone marrow-derived macrophages during S. mansoni infection results in an enhanced TH2 immune response but is also marked by reduced granuloma formation and severely exacerbated disease.
source: While depletion of this immunosuppressive bmMΦ population during S. mansoni infection results in an enhanced TH2 immune response it is also marked by reduced granuloma formation and severely exacerbated disease (Nascimento et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nascimento et al., 2014

claim: PD-L2+ bone marrow-derived macrophages isolated from T. crassiceps infected mice reduce the disease burden during experimental autoimmune encephalitis.
source: A direct host-protective role of these cells is illustrated in a study whereby PD-L2+ bmMΦ isolated from T. crassiceps infected mice reduce the disease burden during experimental autoimmune encephalitis (Terrazas et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Terrazas et al., 2017a

claim: PD-L2 inhibits protective immunity to L. sigmodontis.
source: Although PD-L2 inhibits protective immunity to L. sigmodontis (van der Werf et al., 2013), we were unable to demonstrate that the immunosuppressive capacity of bone-marrow derived M(IL-4) at this time point was due to PD-L2, and suspect that day 35 is too early to see a PD-L2 dependent effect.
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Werf et al., 2013 and experimental data from this study

claim: As S. mansoni infection progresses, PD-L2+ bone marrow-derived macrophages integrate into the resident niche enabling disease resolution.
source: Indeed, as S. mansoni infection progresses, PD-L2+ bmMΦ integrate into the resident niche enabling disease resolution.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge from the literature

claim: In the absence of vitamin A during S. mansoni infection, integration of bone marrow-derived macrophages into the resident niche is inhibited and enhanced mortality pursues.
source: In the absence of vitamin A, integration into the resident niche is inhibited and enhanced mortality pursues (Gundra et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gundra et al., 2017

claim: Monocyte-derived macrophages are critical regulators of host immunity, which can tip the fine balance between infection control and host damage.
source: Together with our data these studies suggest that monocyte-derived macrophages are critical regulators of host immunity, which can tip the fine balance between infection control and host damage.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data and literature

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages upon infiltration into an inflammatory milieu containing IL-4 take on an immunosuppressive phenotype to prevent self-damage associated with more classical inflammatory pathways.
source: As such we hypothesise that bmMΦ upon infiltration into an inflammatory milieu containing IL-4 take on an immunosuppressive phenotype, to prevent self-damage associated with more classical inflammatory pathways.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental data and literature

claim: Similar differences in monocyte recruitment might contribute to susceptibility and resistance between BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice to Leishmania donovani.
source: Of note, similar differences in monocyte recruitment might contribute to susceptibility and resistance between BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice to Leishmania donovani.
evidence: Speculative connection to other disease models

claim: CCR2 dependent monocytes contributed to host susceptibility in BALB/c mice infected with Leishmania donovani.
source: A recent publication by (Terrazas et al., 2017b) demonstrated that CCR2 dependent monocytes contributed to host susceptibility in BALB/c mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Terrazas et al., 2017b

claim: Sato et al., 1999 found no role for CCR2 in mediating resistance in C57BL/6 mice to Leishmania donovani.
source: In contrast, Sato et al., 1999 found no role for CCR2 in mediating resistance in C57BL/6 mice, suggesting that the difference we observed here may be a fundamental difference between these strains that goes beyond helminth infection.
evidence: Supported by reference to Sato et al., 1999

claim: The balance of monocytic versus resident M(IL-4) numbers varies between inbred mouse strains and impacts infection outcome.
source: Thus, the balance of monocytic vs. resident M(IL-4) numbers varies between inbred mouse strains and impacts infection outcome.
evidence: Main conclusion drawn from all experimental data in the study

claim: C57BL/6 mice exhibited a profoundly expanded resident macrophage population during L. sigmodontis infection.
source: C57BL/6 mice exhibited a profoundly expanded resident MΦ (resMΦ) population, which was gradually replenished from the bone marrow in an age-dependent manner.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: The resident macrophage population in C57BL/6 mice was gradually replenished from the bone marrow in an age-dependent manner.
source: C57BL/6 mice exhibited a profoundly expanded resident MΦ (resMΦ) population, which was gradually replenished from the bone marrow in an age-dependent manner.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: Infection status did not alter the bone-marrow derived contribution to the resident macrophage population.
source: Infection status did not alter the bone-marrow derived contribution to the resMΦ population, confirming local proliferation as the driver of resMΦ expansion.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: Local proliferation is the driver of resident macrophage expansion in C57BL/6 mice during L. sigmodontis infection.
source: Infection status did not alter the bone-marrow derived contribution to the resMΦ population, confirming local proliferation as the driver of resMΦ expansion.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: Significantly less resident macrophage expansion was observed in the susceptible BALB/c strain.
source: Significantly less resMΦ expansion was observed in the susceptible BALB/c strain, which instead exhibited an influx of monocytes that assumed an immunosuppressive PD-L2+ phenotype.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: The susceptible BALB/c strain exhibited an influx of monocytes that assumed an immunosuppressive PD-L2+ phenotype.
source: Significantly less resMΦ expansion was observed in the susceptible BALB/c strain, which instead exhibited an influx of monocytes that assumed an immunosuppressive PD-L2+ phenotype.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: Inhibition of monocyte recruitment enhanced nematode killing in BALB/c mice.
source: Inhibition of monocyte recruitment enhanced nematode killing.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data

claim: Both TH2-dependent helminth killing and suppression of the TH2 effector response have been attributed to macrophages activated by IL-4.
source: Both TH2-dependent helminth killing and suppression of the TH2 effector response have been attributed to macrophages (MΦ) activated by IL-4 (M(IL-4)).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge from the literature

claim: Dichotomous functions attributed to M(IL-4) may be explained by whether a macrophage possesses a recently recruited bone marrow-derived macrophage or resident macrophage phenotype upon IL-4Rα stimulation.
source: Through comparison of resistant and susceptible strains during filarial infection we demonstrate that dichotomous functions attributed to M(IL-4) may be explained by whether a MΦ possesses a recently recruited bmMΦ or resMΦ phenotype upon IL-4Rα stimulation.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data
